RSFX 5311 · Fixed Prosthodontics I

Monolithic Zirconia: Adaptation, Adjustment and Polishing

Delivery of the full coverage indirect restoration on #30: four checks in a fixed order, every correction on the right side of the interface, and a polished surface on everything you touched.

Rafael Rocha Pacheco, DDS, MSc, PhDAssociate Dean for Digital Technologies and Associate Professor
Section Director of Dental Materials, Department of Restorative Sciences
Dental College of Georgia at Augusta University

The premise

Contacts, seat, form, bite. Then polish what you touched.

Every bur pass removes glaze, and polishing zirconia back to that gloss is slow work on the hardest material in the mouth. The best adjustment is the one you did not need to make.

The material · Why zirconia BO 1

Three full coverage restorations, three materials, one job

Gold is the reference; metal ceramic hides it under porcelain; monolithic zirconia is one block of polycrystalline ceramic, milled and sintered.

1
Cast goldDuctile: margins burnish, contacts swage. Wears like enamel.
2
Metal ceramicA metal shell for fit and strength, porcelain for colour; the porcelain chips.
3
Monolithic zirconiaOne material, no veneer to chip, tooth coloured; nothing bends, every change is subtractive.

Sources. Images: Glidewell Dental, educational material. [2] Phillips, Ch. 13 and 18. Click any image to enlarge.

The material · From ore to restoration BO 2

Milled like chalk, sintered like stone

Zirconium metal is refined to zirconia powder, pressed into a chalk-like disc, milled oversize at the pre-sintered stage, and only then sintered to full density.

1,300VHN
What you adjust: fully sintered
Vickers hardness about 1,300 VHN, strength above 1,000 MPa. Only diamond cuts it, and every cut must be polished afterwards.4,5
Before
the furnace: what the laboratory adjusts
Contours, contacts and occlusion are shaped pre-sintered. Milling striations survive sintering, so the laboratory polishes before the furnace.4

Sources. [4] Denry and Kelly, Dent Mater 2008. [5] Guazzato et al., Dent Mater 2004.

The material · Sintering BO 2

Milled about 20 percent oversize because sintering shrinks it

1.2136
Enlargement factor
Printed on the lot; the mill scales the design by it.
17.6%
Linear shrinkage
1 minus 1/1.2136, lost in the furnace.
1,500°C
Sintering
To near theoretical density.4
Why this matters at the chair
Fit depends on the laboratory scaling correctly, on an accurate impression or scan, and on a preparation without undercuts. None of those can be fixed by grinding the intaglio.

Sources. [4] Denry and Kelly, Dent Mater 2008. Ivoclar IPS e.max ZirCAD instructions for use. Video: Section of Dental Materials.

The material · Crystal phases BO 3

Yttria holds zirconia in a metastable phase, and stress can let it go

Zr4+O2-Right drag rotates, wheel zooms. Schematic, distortions exaggerated.
3988.906YYttrium[Kr] 4d1 5s2
Tetragonal · t
Kept at room temperature by 3 mol% yttria

The cell is stretched along one axis and the oxygens shift up and down. 3Y-TZP: strong, tough, opaque. This is the phase that transforms under stress.4

Transformation toughening, and its cost
1A crack tip releases the constraint; tetragonal grains there turn monoclinic, expand about 4 % and squeeze the crack shut.4,6
2A coarse bur does the same on purpose: a thin compressive layer (good) over flaws deeper than that layer (bad).7
3Water drives the same change slowly at the surface over years: low temperature degradation.4
Chairside rule
Fine grit, light pressure, water, then polish. Keep the compressive layer, remove the flaws.

Sources. [6] Garvie et al., Nature 1975. [4] Denry and Kelly 2008. [7] Kosmač et al., Dent Mater 1999. [8] Zhang and Lawn 2018.

The material · Transformation toughening BO 3

A crack tip turns tetragonal grains monoclinic, and they squeeze the crack shut

Tetragonal grainTransformed to monoclinic, about 4 % largerCubic grain: cannot transform
1
The crack advances
Stress concentrates at its tip.
2
Grains at the tip transform
Released from the constraint of their neighbours, t grains become m and expand about 4 %.4,6
3
The crack is squeezed shut
The expansion puts the zone around the crack in compression; it stops, or needs much more energy to grow.

Switch to 5Y: cubic grains cannot transform, so the same crack runs through.

Sources. [6] Garvie, Hannink, Pascoe, Nature 1975. [4] Denry and Kelly, Dent Mater 2008. [8] Zhang and Lawn, J Dent Res 2018. Schematic.

The material · Yttria classes BO 4

More yttria buys translucency and spends strength

Cubic grains scatter less light, but they cannot transform, so they do not toughen. Ask the laboratory which class is on the tooth before you rely on a number.

ClassYttriaMicrostructureFlexural strengthTranslucencyTypical use
3Y-TZP3 mol%Tetragonal, fine grains1,000 to 1,200 MPaLowPosterior single units, frameworks, thin monolithic posteriors
4Y-PSZ4 mol%Tetragonal with some cubic700 to 900 MPaMediumMonolithic anterior and posterior, short span
5Y-PSZ5 mol%About half cubic500 to 800 MPaHighAnterior monolithic units; not long spans or thin posterior sections
The ">1,000 MPa" that sells zirconia is a 3Y number.

Sources. [8] Zhang and Lawn, J Dent Res 2018. [9] Vitti, Catelan, Amaral, Pacheco, Advanced Dental Biomaterials 2019.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · Hardness BO 5

Four times harder than enamel, and that is not what wears teeth

Vickers hardness, VHN
What the numbers say
1Zirconia is about four times harder than enamel and twice as hard as lithium disilicate.5,10
2Hardness tells you what cuts it: only diamond, in burs and in rubber polishers.
3It does not tell you what wears the opposing tooth: surface roughness does. Polished zirconia wears enamel about as much as enamel does; ground zirconia, far more.11,12

Hardness is not abrasiveness. Chalk is far softer than slate and still wears it.

Sources. [10] Xu et al., J Dent Res 1998. [5] Guazzato et al. 2004. [11] Janyavula et al., J Prosthet Dent 2013. [12] Preis et al., J Dent 2015.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · The budget BO 1

Stronger is not better for every tooth; match the material to the road

You have 500,000 dollars. You can buy a Ferrari, or you can buy a Caterpillar truck. Which one is stronger? And which one do you drive to school?

Glass-ceramicAbout 400 MPa, stiffness near enamel, polishes and glazes easily, kind to the antagonist. Translucent, sleek, does the job: the right car for a paved commute.
Monolithic zirconiaAbove 1,000 MPa and 210 GPa. If you drive gravel and dirt every day (bruxism, short clinical crowns, a second molar under heavy load), take the truck. On a paved road it does more damage on the way than good.
The lesson
We want restorative materials close to the tooth, not far above it. Choose zirconia when the case needs its strength, and when you do, deliver it polished.

Sources. [2] Phillips, Ch. 18. [3] Lekesiz 2014. [11] Janyavula et al. 2013.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · Definitions BO 6

Finishing decides the surface; polishing only reveals it

Finishing

Removing the defects and scratches left by contouring, with instruments of decreasing grit.2

Polishing

Producing luster on a surface that is already smooth.2

The trap

A polisher cannot remove a 100 µm groove. It rounds the edges and makes it shine: the deepest scratch you left is the roughness you keep.

Average diamond particle size by band colourISO 7711-3
180 µm
SupercoarseBlack
not in the kit
150 µm

100 µm
MediumBlue
40 µm

15 µm

8 µm

2 µm
Polishing paste 
paste on felt
Start at red and never go coarser on zirconia: coarse grit leaves grooves no polisher reaches, and flaws below the compressive layer.

Sources. [2] Phillips, Ch. 16, Table 16-1. ISO 7711-3 colour code. Photographs: R. R. Pacheco.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · Abrasives BO 6 BO 5

Zirconia cannot be cut, only abraded, and only by something harder than it

Abrasive versus substrate, Vickers hardness
Why diamond, and why polishers
1A carbide blade shears; zirconia at 1,300 VHN is harder than the blade, so there is no cutting, only abrasion.2
2The abrasive must be harder than the substrate, and the larger the gap, the faster it works: silica no, alumina barely, diamond yes.2
3That is why the zirconia kit is diamond in rubber: the rubber carries the grains at low speed and light pressure, so each grit erases the last one's scratches without new flaws.7,12

Sources. [2] Phillips, Ch. 16. [7] Kosmač et al. 1999. [12] Preis et al. 2015. Micrographs: R. R. Pacheco.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · The kit BO 7

Diamond in rubber, two grits, never above the rated maximum

Slow speed handpiece, light pressure, keep it moving, air and water between grits. Diamond grit in a rubber binder: the grains abrade, the rubber yields.

DCB4MA 120Diamond wheelØ 12 mm · max 25,000 rpmBulk reduction only
94013 C 170Coarse wheelØ 17 mm · max 10,000 rpmFinish, convex surfaces
94018 C 055Coarse flameØ 5.5 mm · max 10,000 rpmFinish, grooves and margins
94013 F 170Fine wheelØ 17 mm · max 10,000 rpmPolish, convex surfaces
94018 F 055Fine flameØ 5.5 mm · max 10,000 rpmPolish, grooves and margins
1
Reduce
Diamond wheel, or the fine diamond bur with water. Bulk change only, light pressure.
2
Finish: coarse (C)
Wheel for convex surfaces, flame for grooves and embrasures. At most 10,000 rpm.
3
Polish: fine (F)
Same shapes, same cap. Aim for the gloss of the untouched glaze beside it.

Sources. Instrument data: Komet Dental catalogue. Photographs: R. R. Pacheco.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · As you do it BO 7

Mark, reduce, re-mark; then finish and polish, cleaning between every grit

Between every grit, every time
Air and water, then dry. One coarse grain carried into the fine step scratches the surface you are polishing, and gloss can only be judged on a clean, dry surface.
1
Mark
With the thinnest film that shows it: AccuFilm for contacts, Bausch 40 µm for occlusion.
2
Reduce, then re-mark
Fine diamond or coarse polisher, wet, light. Remove only the mark; three small passes beat one large one.
3
Finish, then polish
Coarse (C) erases the scratches, fine (F) brings the gloss. Compare against the glaze next to it.

Sources. [2] Phillips, Ch. 16: rinse between grits. [12] Preis et al., J Dent 2015. Photographs: Pacheco RR, Section of Dental Materials; polishers, Section of Fixed Prosthodontics.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · Why polish BO 8

A rough surface collects plaque and grinds the tooth it meets

0.2µm
Plaque threshold
Ra above which bacterial retention rises.13
>1µm
Ground
Ra after a fine diamond, before polishing.12
<0.2µm
Polished
Ra with the fine diamond-rubber polisher.12
Polished beats glazed
1Glaze is a thin glass skin; it wears through in months of function, then enamel meets whatever is underneath.11
2Polished zirconia: the lowest enamel wear of the finishes tested, below glazed and far below ground.11,12
3Ground, unpolished: highest enamel wear and the lowest strength. The one finish you never deliver.7,12

Sources. [13] Bollen CM, Lambrechts P, Quirynen M. Comparison of surface roughness of oral hard materials to the threshold surface roughness for bacterial plaque retention: a review of the literature. Dent Mater 1997;13(4):258-269 (photograph). [11] Janyavula et al. 2013. [12] Preis et al. 2015.

Finishing and polishing zirconia · The rule BO 7 BO 8

Polishing zirconia is slow and hard. So adjust as little as possible.

Why it is hardOnly diamond polishes it. Each grit must erase the last one's scratches, at 10,000 rpm and light pressure, on 1,300 VHN. A ground cusp tip takes minutes to bring back to gloss.
Why it is not optionalThe first bur pass removes the glaze. Underneath is rough zirconia, which wears enamel faster than polished zirconia or enamel itself.11,12
What minimal looks likeNever a sweep. Mark with the thinnest film, remove only the mark, re-mark. Big fit corrections belong to the preparation, never to the intaglio.

Sources. [11] Janyavula et al. 2013. [12] Preis et al. 2015. [7] Kosmač et al. 1999.

The session · Armamentarium BO 9

What you receive, and what goes back in the bag

On your bench
1Prepared yellow tooth #30. Replaces #30 in your dentoform; the restoration was made for this preparation.
2Unprepared #29 and #31. Your proximal contacts; damage to them is graded as damage to adjacent teeth.
3Zirconia restoration for #30. Glazed, as delivered from the laboratory.
4Bur block, one per pair, plus the fine diamond football and small round diamond from your kit.
5Also: fit-checking silicone, mineral oil (typodont only).

Sources. Photographs: Section of Dental Materials, Dental College of Georgia at Augusta University. Product images: manufacturers.

The session · The order BO 9

Four checks in this order, with a stop after each one

The order is not a convention. Each step only makes sense once the previous one is right, and every earlier change moves the occlusal surface.

1
Proximal contacts
A tight contact holds the restoration up. Until it is relieved, nothing else can be judged. AccuFilm, then floss.
2
Internal adaptation
Now it can seat. Find what binds, correct the preparation, confirm the margin. Fit checker, explorer.
3
External form
Fully seated, the emergence and embrasures are finally where they will be. Explorer, floss.
4
Occlusion, then polish
Last, because every earlier change moves it. Bausch paper, Shimstock, then polish everything you touched.
After each check: STOP
Call faculty, get the step approved and signed, then move to the next. An unapproved step is redone, not improved later. And after every adjustment that touched the restoration comes polishing, before the next check.

Sources. [1] Shillingburg et al., Fundamentals of Fixed Prosthodontics, 4th ed., Ch. 28.

The session · Marking media BO 10

Pick the medium by its thickness, because thickness is what it measures

8µm
Shimstock
Holds or slips. The only one thin enough to verify a contact; it does not mark.
21µm
AccuFilm
Proximal contacts. Passes a correct contact, marks only the tight one.
40µm
Bausch paper
Occlusal marking in closure and in excursions.
72µm
Horseshoe paper
Too thick for adjustment: it marks cusps that are not touching.
Why the thick paper lies
A 72 µm paper marks a cusp that is 50 µm short of contact, so you grind what was never high. A 21 µm film marks only the contact that is tight, and 8 µm Shimstock tells you whether the bite holds.

Sources. Thicknesses from the manufacturers' labels.

Checkpoints BO 9 BO 12 BO 13 BO 18

What faculty checks at each stop, so you can check it first

Stop 1 · Contacts
1Passes: both contacts present by eye; waxed floss snaps through with slight resistance, no shredding; contact in the occlusal third; adjusted surface glossy.
2Back: floss shreds or hangs; passes with no resistance; contact at the ridge or gingival.
Stop 2 · Adaptation
1Passes: seats with finger pressure, no rock; explorer passes both ways; even silicone with a continuous margin band; correction made on the preparation.
2Back: rocks; explorer catches; show-through on a wall; any grinding on the intaglio (critical).
Stop 3 · Form
1Passes: emergence continuous with the root; no overhang or ledge; embrasure open to floss; polished to the gloss of the glaze.
2Back: explorer catches apically; floss hangs; dull surface.
Stop 4 · Occlusion and polish
1Passes: Bausch marks match the neighbours; no excursive streaks absent on the canine; Shimstock holds on restoration, neighbours and canine; every ground surface glossy.
2Back: restoration marks alone; no marks; canine lets go; matte or flattened table.
Aim in this order
No damage to #29 and #31, no grinding on the intaglio, a seated restoration, then contacts, then occlusion, then gloss. The first two cannot be recovered; everything after them can.
